about: Every defect found in this repository from inside it, with the mechanism that found it and the test that keeps it found. This file is data: scripts/figures.py counts it and checks that every test named here is one pytest actually collects, so the number in the README cannot drift from the repository the way a typed figure does. Two entries are not defects in the shipped tool and say so: one was the eval measuring the cost of a policy, one was a defect in the measuring apparatus. They are here because they were found the same way everything else was.

found_by_meanings.test suite: a test that was written for something else failed
found_by_meanings.adversarial engineering review: the code read as an attacker would read it, looking for the call that never happens
found_by_meanings.adversarial legal review: the governance catalogue read against the Official Journal
found_by_meanings.fuzzing: coverage-guided mutation over every parser, deterministic seeds
found_by_meanings.benign corpus: the half of the eval corpus that must not fail
found_by_meanings.real-serialiser corpus: artifacts written by torch, safetensors, onnx and h5py rather than crafted
found_by_meanings.benchmark self-tests: the tests that check the comparison is fair to the other tools
found_by_meanings.exhaustive sweep: every input in a bounded space, not a sample
found_by_meanings.reading the tool's own output: running it on a real artifact and looking at what came back
found_by_meanings.running the harness: a figure the harness printed that could not be true
found_by_meanings.external adversarial audit: the repository read by someone outside it, looking for the claim the code does not check
found_by_meanings.running the gate: `make lint`, `make test` or `make fuzz` refused the working tree
found_by_meanings.product review against a roadmap: the repository read against a written plan for what it should become, looking for the place the plan's first requirement was already violated
found_by_meanings.writing a test for an adjacent feature: a test written for something new asserted, for the first time, on a value the old code had always produced incorrectly
found_by_meanings.adversarial review of new code: the modules written for this release read back as an attacker would read them, before the release, looking for the path the tests were written around
found_by_meanings.using the tool as a person would: the commands run end to end against a workspace written the way somebody would write it, rather than the way the fixtures do

defects.title: The zip branch never cleared fully_read
defects.effect: An archive over the member budget, or one that would not open, reached PASS with the unscanned members never looked at.

defects.title: verify_package returned ok=True against non-matching anchors
defects.effect: A green result printed next to the words "this key is not one of yours".

defects.title: The harness tamper check passed vacuously on 8 of 50
defects.effect: The tampered package was byte-identical to the original whenever the recorded verdict already equalled the constant the mutation wrote.
defects.not_shipped_because: a defect in the measuring apparatus, not in the tool
defects.pinned_note: the mutation is a named function now, `harness.tampered_entry`, so the property that made this defect possible - that it must never rewrite an entry to itself - is asserted directly instead of living in a comment beside one line

defects.title: Five false positives on the benign corpus
defects.effect: _codecs.encode and numpy._core.numeric._frombuffer failed five real state_dicts under the strict allowlist.
defects.not_shipped_because: the eval measuring the cost of a policy, resolved as two documented risk acceptances

defects.title: ACT-GGF-004 could never fire
defects.effect: A rule with catalogue entries in two languages, unreachable by construction: the tensor loop guaranteed the counts it compared.

defects.title: A seven-byte pickle gate let a protocol 0 gadget through
defects.effect: posix.system inside a checkpoint reached PASS with exit 0 under both policies. The analyser was fine; it was never called.

defects.title: The torch. prefix allowed its own executable siblings
defects.effect: cpp_extension.load_inline, torch._C, torch.multiprocessing.spawn and torch.hub were allowed by prefix, with six hand-written exceptions that did not cover them.

defects.title: Fourteen parser bugs, including 73 seconds and 8.1 million objects from 24 bytes
defects.effect: Exponential recursion, unbounded allocation, uncaught exceptions, reports that could not be serialised, and five separate paths to PASS on an artifact that was never read.

defects.title: The legacy torch container failed as a false positive
defects.effect: Every checkpoint written before torch 1.6 reached FAIL on ACT-PKL-010: the format is four concatenated pickles by design.

defects.title: The benchmark counted declines in the detection denominator
defects.effect: Every rival's score was understated, and the error direction favoured Actaira every time, which is why it survived a reading.
defects.not_shipped_because: a defect in the measuring apparatus, not in the tool

defects.title: The consistency proof failed for every power-of-two old_size
defects.effect: Prover and verifier were written from the same misunderstanding, agreed with each other, and disagreed with RFC 6962.

defects.title: Every attestation restarted the chain from genesis
defects.effect: --extends could never succeed, because the ledger it was meant to extend was rebuilt from nothing on each run. A log you restart is not a log.

defects.title: An archive member was decompressed without a size limit
defects.effect: A 400 KiB archive holding a 400 MiB member made the inspector allocate 400 MiB: a denial of service against the machine doing the auditing.

defects.title: Two package members under one name defeated the manifest
defects.effect: A zip may carry the same name twice and read returns the last one, so an unsigned member could hide behind a name the manifest covered: every hash matched and nothing showed as undeclared.

defects.title: A decompression bomb was rated MEDIUM and reached PASS
defects.effect: An artifact that expands without bound is a denial of service against whoever loads it, and at the default threshold a MEDIUM does not fail an artifact.

defects.title: A pickle concatenated after the first STOP was never analysed
defects.effect: genops stops at the first STOP, so a benign pickle with a gadget appended produced zero findings.

defects.title: STACK_GLOBAL went unresolved without a model of the memo
defects.effect: From protocol 4 the pickler memoises the module string and re-pushes it with BINGET, so a scanner without a memo loses the operands of every repeated import and reports them as undecidable.

defects.title: Tensor storages were reported one finding each
defects.effect: A real state_dict uses BINPERSID once per storage, so a fifty-tensor model produced fifty identical lines and whatever else the scan found was below them.

defects.title: Storages inside a legacy container were rated MEDIUM
defects.effect: A nested stream cannot see the container it is in, so every pre-1.6 checkpoint carried a yellow line for using the mechanism its own format documents.

defects.title: The catalogue described the Digital Omnibus as unpublished
defects.effect: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 had been in the Official Journal for six weeks, and the tool printed advice to keep preparing for the deadline it had moved.

defects.title: Article 4 was taught in its repealed wording
defects.effect: The catalogue asked for evidence of a level of AI literacy attained, which the amended article expressly does not require.

defects.title: Annex IV was cited at the wrong point
defects.effect: Point 5 is the risk management system; the catalogue cited it as validation and testing, which is point 2(g), and disclaimed the content of point 5 two lines later.

defects.title: The new Article 5 prohibitions were missing
defects.effect: Points (ba) and (bb), inserted by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 and applying from 2 December 2026, were the only duty in the catalogue with a date between then and the end of the year, and it was not there.

defects.title: The Article 111(3) transitional was missing
defects.effect: GPAI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 have until 2 August 2027, and the catalogue applied the earlier date to all of them.

defects.title: Article 53(1)(b) was rated as fully supported
defects.effect: A signed BOM of artifacts is not the documentation a downstream provider needs, and rating it SUPPORTS was the tool claiming one obligation it does not carry.

defects.title: Article 12 was claimed by a ledger of artifact inspections
defects.effect: Article 12 asks the high-risk system to record its own events. A record of this tool's inspections is not that, and the evidence map pointed three kinds of evidence at it.

defects.title: The web panel kept a PROVISIONAL notice after nothing was provisional
defects.effect: The banner was emitted unconditionally, so the panel warned about a status no row carried any more.

defects.title: torch.storage._load_from_bytes was on the allowlist
defects.effect: Its body is torch.load(BytesIO(b), weights_only=False), a full unpickler with the safe mode off. A gadget in the byte operand reached PASS with exit 0 under both policies, and a test asserted the entry was correct.

defects.title: A protocol 2 payload handed to a nested loader could not be followed
defects.effect: Protocol 2 has no byte-string opcode, so the pickler writes bytes as _codecs.encode(text, latin1) and the payload arrived as the result of a call. A known gadget was downgraded to an unknown one for the price of passing protocol=2.

defects.title: One byte after STOP removed an archive member from the analysis
defects.effect: An ambiguously named member was kept only when its bytes looked like a pickle at both ends, so appending a byte made it fail the tail check and be dropped with no rule at all, leaving fully_read True and the verdict PASS.

defects.title: Trailing zero padding was passed over in silence
defects.effect: Padding after the final STOP never reaches the unpickler, so failing on it would be noise, but saying nothing made the report read as though the whole file had been analysed.

defects.title: The assessment printed a capability as though it were evidence
defects.effect: The catalogue's "what Actaira provides" lines were printed under the word provides for every applicable obligation, evidence or none, so a run that established nothing read like a run that had.

defects.title: The concatenated-stream budget failed open
defects.effect: The walker stops after eight trailing streams and simply left the loop: no finding, `truncated` never set, `fully_read` still True. A legacy magic number to suppress the concatenation finding, eight one-byte fillers to exhaust the budget and a gadget as stream nine gave a 115-byte file an empty findings list, max_severity None, PASS and exit 0 under both policies, while any consumer that loads more than one object from the stream runs os.system.

defects.title: A MARK-built tuple kept only its last element
defects.effect: `stack_before` is listed bottom to top, and the walk read every entry as if it sat above the mark: it popped one slice item as a fixed operand, never popped the container below the mark, and discarded the rest of the slice. TUPLE, which is what a pickler emits for more than three arguments, produced a one-element tuple holding the last argument, so a payload handed to a nested loader in any position but the last was invisible to the nested-loader check.

defects.title: GLOBAL's module and name were split from the left
defects.effect: `pickletools` renders GLOBAL's two newline-terminated fields joined by a space, so a module name containing a space had its first token read as the module and everything after it as the callable. Not exploitable, because such a module cannot be imported, and fixed because a scanner that reports a callable the file does not name is wrong in the direction that matters least until the day it is not.

defects.title: INST imported a callable and was never judged
defects.effect:
INST carries module and name inline exactly as GLOBAL does and reaches find_class at load time exactly as GLOBAL does, but it lived only in EXECUTION_OPCODES, where it was counted and never passed to the policy. Twenty-seven bytes of protocol 0, (S'echo PWNED'
ios
system
., ran a denylisted callable and passed under both policies with one INFO line. The design note at the top of the module enumerates the import primitives and forgot this one.

defects.title: A tail the walker could not measure was dropped in silence
defects.effect: Real pickle reads I\\x00\\n. as the integer 0 followed by STOP where pickletools raises on it, so the trailing-stream walker could not compute the stream's length and returned, while the parse error that would have shown it was suppressed by the torch legacy exemption. A 48-byte file with an os.system gadget behind that divergence reached PASS with exit 0, and a repeated-load consumer ran it. The exemption is now bounded to the storage region, whose position is measured from a checkpoint torch wrote.

defects.title: An RFC 3161 token whose signature was never checked read as a verified one
defects.effect: `signature_state: not_verified` - no certificate in the token, an algorithm this verifier does not implement, or anything the two broad `except` clauses in `_check_signature` swallowed - was accepted by `ok` exactly as `embedded_cert_only` was. The one field a caller looks at could not tell a checked token from an unchecked one, in a module whose docstring ends "Never say verified about something that was not".

defects.title: manifest.tsr was covered by no signature at all
defects.effect: The token cannot appear in `files` - it is issued over the manifest's pending form - and that was read as "cannot be covered", so it sat outside the file list and outside the Ed25519 signature. The only cross-checks were the genTime and the serial the manifest advertises, both of which a second token minted with the same values satisfies, and Actaira verifies no TSA chain. Swapping the token needed no key and left every check green.

defects.title: --extends returned before verification, so every trust flag was ignored in silence
defects.effect: `actaira verify NEW --extends OLD` ran the consistency proof and returned, never reaching `verify_package`. `--require-trust` and `--trusted-keyring` were parsed, accepted and discarded: a package signed by a key the caller had explicitly said they did not accept exited 0.

defects.title: A trust anchor that would not load was indistinguishable from no anchor
defects.effect: A keyring with `key` for `keys`, a `keys` that was a string, an empty `keys`, or `--pubkey ""` all produced an empty anchor set, which fell through to the `embedded_key_only` branch: OK, exit 0, and the caller's assertion about whose signatures they accept dropped without a word - along with every revocation that keyring carried. An unparseable `--pubkey` propagated a ValueError out of the verifier instead.

defects.title: A manifest claiming rfc3161 with no timestamp block compared every field with itself
defects.effect: `declared.get("gen_time") not in (None, actual)` and `str(declared.get("serial_number", actual)) != str(actual)` both pass when the block is absent, and `timestamp_subject` strips the block so removing it does not change what the TSA signed. A token issued in 1999 over the right digest verified and was reported as third-party time evidence.

defects.title: The no-score guard read keys and never values
defects.effect: The guard on the governance layer's thesis walked dictionary keys only, and only through dicts and lists. "Actaira rates this obligation 87% compliant (grade B, overall score 4.2/5)" in `governance.AIA-4.summary` left all 172 governance tests green while every rendering printed a grade. It also missed an integer under a neutral key (`readiness_index: 87`), stepped over tuples, and was applied to the assessment dictionary alone - not to `governance clock --json`, the text renders, the dossier, the catalogues or the web routes.

defects.title: The dossier's subject digest was written and never read
defects.effect: `governance/pack.py` files the dossier under the digest of the artifact set it covers and repeats that set as `subjects`; nothing in `attest/` read either. The naive forgery breaks `prev_hash` and was caught, but re-linking - appending the stolen dossier through `chain.append` onto another package's inspections - recomputes every link, the Merkle root, the head and the signature, and verified clean with the assessment now sitting at the end of a chain it was never computed from.

defects.title: The fuzzer published its argument as a measurement
defects.effect: `"iters": config.iters` is the number on the command line. The worker had always written the real count to `state/worker.json` and nobody read it, and `except Exception: break` on a worker that died without leaving state finished the run silently - so a run that executed twelve cases published the full figure, zero findings and exit 0, and `scripts/figures.py` summed those figures into the README.
defects.not_shipped_because: a defect in the measuring apparatus, not in the tool

defects.title: The fuzzer's soundness oracle was circular, and its rule list had drifted
defects.effect: Property (d), "never PASS over something it did not read whole", re-derived PASS from `fully_read` - the same boolean `decide_verdict` produced PASS from, three lines earlier in the same function. And `fuzz.UNREAD_RULE_IDS` was a copy of `inspect.UNREAD_RULE_IDS` missing ACT-PKL-013, so the fuzzer could not have seen a PASS beside the rule DEF-33 was fixed to emit.
defects.not_shipped_because: a defect in the measuring apparatus, not in the tool

defects.title: Archive members the name gate rejected were never mentioned
defects.effect: The gate decides which members are opened, and everything it rejected - storage blobs, the version marker, anything a repackager had renamed - was absent from the report entirely: no rule, no metadata, and `fully_read: true` beside a PASS. This is the other half of DEF-01: the budget and the unreadable member were fixed, the members nobody tried to read were not.

defects.title: The benchmark read picklescan's error flag before its detections
defects.effect: `scan_err` was tested first, so a run that both found a gadget and hit a member it could not open was recorded as "declined" - which drops the artifact out of the detection denominator. Every one of those moved the comparison in this project's favour, which is the single direction a benchmark written by the vendor must never be wrong in.
defects.not_shipped_because: a defect in the benchmark that compares the tool, not in the tool

defects.title: The harness printed its positive control and never asserted it
defects.effect: The tamper gate asked only that no tampered package be accepted, which is trivially true when no package is accepted either. A signing layer that rejected everything, untouched packages included, exited 0 with `0/50 packages verified before tampering` printed one line above.
defects.not_shipped_because: a defect in the measuring apparatus, not in the tool

defects.title: A control character in a member name destroyed the whole JUnit report
defects.effect: XML 1.0 cannot represent a C0 control, escaped or otherwise. `ElementTree` wrote the byte out and every parser then rejected the document, so one member called `weights\u0001.bin` inside one artifact cost the entire report rather than one line of it - and a runner shows a report it cannot parse as no tests at all, which is the silent pass the three-verdict mapping exists to prevent.

defects.title: Every ML-BOM was invalid against the CycloneDX version it declared
defects.effect: `modelCard.modelParameters` is declared with `additionalProperties: false` and a closed field list, and this emitted a `properties` array inside it. Tools that do not validate accepted the document, which is why it shipped; tools that do rejected all of it. Separately, `bom-ref` was derived from the digest alone, so one document covering the same bytes twice - a file and a copy of it in one directory - carried two components under one reference.

defects.title: Four limits the local server did not have, and one set on the wrong object
defects.effect: `verify_package` read every package member with `ZipFile.read`, which decompresses without limit, so a 1.4 MiB package posted to `/api/verify` allocated gigabytes. A multipart part could carry unbounded headers and a request unbounded parts and field names, each capped individually and never counted. And `_Server.timeout` was read by `handle_request()`, which `serve_forever()` never calls, so the slowloris bound it was written for did not exist. Neither `Origin` nor `Host` was checked, leaving CSRF through the operator's browser and DNS rebinding open.

defects.title: safety_results.json was tracked and rewritten by every benchmark run
defects.effect: fickling appends its scan output to it on each `make benchmark`, so a benchmark run produced a 300 KB diff of another tool's output on top of the previous run's. Reviewing it told a reader nothing, and it was the only run artifact in the repository that was not ignored.
defects.not_shipped_because: repository hygiene, not a fault in the tool
defects.pinned_note: the release gate asserts both halves, the ignore rule and the index, and the test breaks the ignore rule in a copy of the tree to prove the gate can fail on it

defects.title: `discover` printed the hosts of the listing, not the hosts of the run
defects.effect: The one command in this tool that touches the network prints what it contacted, and the line was filled from `Discovery.hosts_contacted`, a snapshot taken before any artifact was fetched. A `--fetch` over a manifest of URLs therefore downloaded from those hosts and then printed "none; nothing was contacted", because the manifest itself is a local file and the listing had reached nobody. The same line was wrong in the milder direction for every remote source: it named the API host and never the CDN the bytes actually came from. `stage()` already returns the client's cumulative host list, so the fix was to print that when there was a fetch.

defects.title: The one HTTP client followed a redirect from https to http, and did not record where it went
defects.effect: `Http` documents two properties: HTTPS only, and a record of every host contacted. `urlopen` broke both through its default redirect handler. A source answering with a 302 to an `http://` URL had its artifact fetched in plaintext by a client whose docstring says it refuses to do that, and the host that actually served the bytes never entered `hosts_contacted`, so `actaira discover` printed the redirector and not the server. Confirmed against CPython before fixing: the downgrade is followed with no warning. The client now builds its own opener with no HTTP handler at all, refuses a redirect to any scheme but https, and records every hop it follows.

defects.title: A credential followed a redirect to a different host
defects.effect: `HTTPRedirectHandler` copies the original request's headers onto the redirected one, `Authorization` included. The two connectors most likely to carry a token are exactly the two whose downloads redirect across a host boundary: a GitHub release asset redirects to `objects.githubusercontent.com`, a HuggingFace resolve URL redirects to the LFS CDN. So a `GITHUB_TOKEN` set for `api.github.com` was handed to a second service on every asset fetch, silently, from a package whose stated rule is that credentials come from one named variable and go to one named source. The header is now dropped on any hop that changes host, which costs nothing: both redirect targets serve presigned URLs.

defects.title: The HuggingFace URL parser read an owner called `tree` as a view marker
defects.effect: A Hub browser URL carries the view after the repository (`/tree/main`, `/blob/main/config.json`), and the parser looked for those words anywhere in the path rather than past the owner and the name. `hf://tree/model` therefore truncated to nothing and was reported to the operator as a URL that does not name a repository. The GitHub parser beside it already searched from index 2, which is how the asymmetry was noticed: two parsers doing the same job, one of them more careful.
defects.not_shipped_because: found by reading the two URL parsers against each other before this package had a release; it is recorded because the mechanism that caught it is the one this ledger is a claim about

defects.title: The connector contract did not pass the repository's own linter
defects.effect: `src/actaira/connectors/model.py` arrived with two `S310` findings: the `noqa` sat on the `urlopen` call and ruff flags the `Request` construction beside it. `make lint` is one of the six steps in `make all`, so the package could not have been merged with the gate green. The suppression now sits where the finding is and carries the argument for it, which is that `_guard` has already refused every scheme but https on the line above.
defects.not_shipped_because: a lint failure on an unreleased module, caught by the gate that exists for it
defects.pinned_note: held down by `make lint`, which runs ruff over src, tests, evals, fuzz and scripts on every commit; there is nothing in the tool's behaviour for a unit test to assert

defects.title: The archive member gate decided by name, so a pickle called `data/0` was never opened
defects.effect: Members were selected for scanning by their names: `.pkl`, `.pickle`, `data.pkl` always, `.bin`/`.ckpt`/`.pt`/`.pth` when ambiguous. Everything else was listed as skipped and left closed. A repackager who names a payload `archive/data/0` - which is exactly what PyTorch calls a raw storage blob - got a report with no pickle findings, no imported callables and no mention of the gadget. The artifact was INCONCLUSIVE, but so was every clean checkpoint, so nothing distinguished them, and `--allow-inconclusive` (which teams set because clean checkpoints were inconclusive) turned it into exit 0. D-06 has said since the first release that an extension is a claim and the bytes are the fact; the gate inside the archive was still asking the attacker.

defects.title: A directory walk filtered by file extension, so a pickle named `notes.txt` was invisible
defects.effect: `collect_paths()` kept only files whose suffix was in `ARTIFACT_SUFFIXES`. Scanning a directory therefore never saw a pickle called `weights`, `notes.txt` or `model.safetensors.bak`: not scanned, not reported, not counted. The tool's own detector classifies by content and has since 0.1.0; the walk one level above it asked the file name. Same defect class as DEF-59, one level out.

defects.title: One `fully_read` boolean made every clean checkpoint INCONCLUSIVE
defects.effect: `fully_read` had to answer two unrelated questions: did every parser finish, and was the whole file examined. Nothing examines the whole file, so ACT-ZIP-007 - which fires on every archive carrying storage blobs, that is, all of them - took the verdict of every clean PyTorch checkpoint to INCONCLUSIVE and `actaira scan` to exit 3. The available response was `--allow-inconclusive` in CI, which also suppressed the artifacts whose headers genuinely would not parse. A signal that fires on every input is not a signal, and this one was hiding the ones that mattered.

defects.title: `read_bytes()[:LIMIT]` in four places, which is not a limit
defects.effect: The whole file was in memory by the time the slice ran, so a 4 GB declaration file allocated 4 GB and then kept 64 KiB of it. The bound was written, reviewed and merged and it protected nothing. Two parsers had no bound at all: a raw `.pkl` and a GGUF were both read whole, and a quantised 70B GGUF is tens of gigabytes. Actaira is pointed at files an adversary produced and is usually run in CI, so a file that exhausts the auditor's memory is a cheap and completely reliable way to avoid being audited.

defects.title: A self-signed certificate was returned as its own issuer, so the path walk looped
defects.effect: `_find_issuer` fell back to returning the certificate itself when it was self-signed, and the walk had already checked the store before looking for an issuer. A token whose root was not one of the caller's anchors therefore looped on that root until the path-length cap and reported 'the certificate path is longer than 8' - for what is really 'this root is not one of yours'. The answer was correct and the reason sent the reader to the wrong fix.
defects.not_shipped_because: the code it was in never reached a release: chain validation is new in this version and the loop was found by the negative-control test written alongside it, before the first tag that carries the module

defects.title: The release gate's own test count check could not fail
defects.effect: `_collect_count` parsed pytest's output for a line reading 'N tests collected'. This project sets `-q` in addopts, so `-q --collect-only` sees two and prints per-file totals with no grand total: the regex never matched, the function returned None, and the caller skipped the comparison. The check printed a green tick on every tree, including one where the suite would not import. Found by the test written to prove the gate could fail, which is the only thing that finds a check like this.
defects.not_shipped_because: the gate is new in this version and the hole was found by its own negative-control test before the tag

defects.title: The policy layer read a trust field that does not exist, so every keyring meant DENY
defects.effect: `_attestation_claims` turned an `actaira verify` result into the claims a policy sees, and it read `key_trusted` then `trusted`. The result carries neither: the field is `trust_state`, with three values - trusted, untrusted, embedded_key_only. Both lookups missed, `bool(None)` is False, and every run that supplied a trusted keyring came back DENY with `signer_trusted: actual false` printed beside a package the verifier had just called trusted. The three states are the whole point of this layer, and the bridge between the two halves collapsed them into one. Found by running the two commands end to end against each other rather than by a test of either.
defects.not_shipped_because: the policy layer is new in this version and the bridge was exercised end to end before the tag

defects.title: A colon with no space after it made every scope a stringified dictionary
defects.effect: `miniyaml` decided a line was a mapping with `":" in text` and split it with `partition(":")`. YAML opens a value only when the colon is followed by a space or ends the line, which is why `jira:write`, `sha256:aaaa` and `http://example.com` are scalars in every real parser. Here `- jira:write` became `{"jira": "write"}`, the agent loader stringified it, and the shipped example's A-BOM published `"{'jira': 'write'}"` where the declaration said `jira:write`. A scope is exactly the field a reviewer compares between two releases, so the A-BOM was wrong in the one place it is read most carefully. Nothing caught it because no test had ever asserted on a scope's value - the declaration loaded, the digest was stable, and the output was consistently wrong.
defects.found_by: writing a test for an adjacent feature

defects.title: `python -m actaira.cli` ran main() halfway through defining the module
defects.effect: The `if __name__ == "__main__"` guard had drifted into the middle of `cli.py`, above roughly a thousand lines of command handlers. Running the package as a module executed `main()` at that point, so argument parsing succeeded and dispatch died with `NameError: name '_run_agent' is not defined`. defects.title: A source that returned to an earlier state reported the same change forever

defects.title: Cycle detection systematically under-reported, in two different ways

defects.title: The version this tool told every remote host was frozen two minor releases back

defects.title: `state-export/v1` published two arrays nothing could ever fill

A consumer written against a published contract was reading a field the producer could not populate. Fixed by wiring the writes rather than by removing the field, because a v1 consumer already reads it and the compatibility promise says a published contract stays published (D-233).

defects.title: A dead function whose docstring named two callers that do not exist

defects.title: A reader that stopped reading produced a traceback and exit 0
defects.effect: `actaira schema | head -3`, and the same with `less`, `grep -m` or any consumer that stops early, printed a `BrokenPipeError` traceback to stderr and exited 0. Every command in this tool prints more lines than such a reader consumes, so it was every command. The exit code is the part that matters: a stack trace on stderr with a success code is what a CI job shows the person debugging it, from the tool that has just reported that nothing failed. Found by running the quickstart against the installed wheel rather than the checkout, which is where a shell pipeline actually gets used. Fixed by catching it at the entry point, pointing stdout at the null device so the interpreter's own flush has nothing left to fail on, and exiting 141, the shell's convention for SIGPIPE (D-235).
defects.found_by: using the tool as a person would

defects.title: The nightly asserted the behaviour 2.2 deliberately replaced, and only the nightly runs it
defects.effect: `tests/test_real_artifacts.py` and the expectation recorded by `evals/corpus/real.py` both said a benign `torch.save` zip comes back INCONCLUSIVE with `fully_read` False. Every other test moved with the change; these two did not, because they need torch, onnx, h5py and safetensors and therefore run only in the nightly. The release would have shipped with its own nightly red and its recorded expectations describing the previous release. Found by installing the real ML stack and running the nightly with skipping disallowed, which §6 of the closing plan asks for and which had not been done since the change.

defects.title: The fuzz harness imported a POSIX-only module at module scope, and the suite imports the fuzz harness
defects.effect: `fuzz/fuzz_targets.py` imported `resource` unconditionally. `tests/test_fuzz_regressions.py` loads that file by path to check the instrument against the product, so on a platform without `resource` the import error interrupted collection and the entire suite refused to run: 41 tests absent, and the only thing that noticed was `make release-check`, which compared 3161 tests in figures.json against 3120 collected and could not say why. A gate that a reader cannot run on their machine is a gate that gets taken on trust. The conditional import is half the fix; the other half is that `RLIMIT_AS` and `SIGALRM` enforce two of the four promises the fuzzer makes, so a platform without them runs a weaker instrument and every summary now names which oracles were not enforced rather than printing `0 property violation(s)` as though four still held.
defects.not_shipped_because: the fuzz harness is not part of the distributed package; it is the apparatus that measures it, and this is a defect in the apparatus and in what the apparatus was willing to claim

defects.title: The platform separator reached documents built to be compared across machines
defects.effect: "The last path segment of a report path" was spelled three ways in one codebase. `Path(p).name` in three places, `p.replace(chr(92), '/').rsplit('/', 1)[-1]` in three more, and the POSIX-only `p.rsplit('/', 1)[-1]` in six: the ML-BOM component name, the receipt's subject rows, the governance dossier's `artifacts_not_fully_read`, the assessed-artifact list, the bundle location and the CLI's summary line. On a platform whose separator is not '/', every one of those six documents carried the producer's full absolute path where a filename belonged - inside a document that is signed, published and meant to be comparable with the same document produced on another machine. `src/actaira/web/server.py` had a docstring explaining exactly why both separators have to be cut; six call sites in the same tree did not do it. Now one helper, `actaira.model.artifact_name` (D-238), and the call sites are the helper. The second site is the filesystem connector's listing, which built each artifact path with `str(Path.relative_to(root))`: the same directory listed on two machines produced two discoveries that no longer compared equal, and the separator it emitted off POSIX is also an escape character inside the JSON it is written into. That one is `as_posix()`; the local absolute path, which is genuinely platform-shaped, stays in `extra` where nothing compares it.

defects.title: The tensor table clipped a number mid-digit on a phone, and the clipped value still read as a number
defects.effect: Four columns do not fit a 400px viewport. `.tablewrap` carried `overflow-x: auto`, so the table could be scrolled, but a horizontal scrollbar inside a card is close to invisible and nothing indicated the row continued. A tensor of 65 536 elements therefore rendered as `65.5` and the `ELEMENTS` header as `ELEMENT`. A truncated label is a cosmetic problem; a truncated number that still looks like a number is a wrong figure shown to a reader with nothing to notice, in a tool whose whole argument is that its output is checkable. Below 560px the rows are cards now, each cell behind the translated column name, and nothing is clipped. Found by looking at the phone capture that `make screenshots` takes and that nothing displayed - which is the reason that capture is taken, and the first time in this repository it paid for itself.

defects.title: The action's entrypoint flattened one input out of five before writing them into GITHUB_OUTPUT
defects.effect: `GITHUB_OUTPUT` is a key=value file, one line per output, so a newline inside a value writes a line the script never emitted. The script knew this and said so in a comment - and applied the defence to `path` alone. `sarif-file` reached the writer untouched on both the normal path and the not-found early exit, so an input of `x` followed by a newline and `should-fail=false` set the output the action's own last step reads to decide whether the job fails: a scan that found a critical finding, reported as a job that passed. `policy`, `fail-on` and `allow-inconclusive` were unvalidated and unflattened too, and reached the GitHub step summary, where a newline injects arbitrary markdown. Every input is now flattened once, at the top, before anything reads it; the three with a closed set of values are checked against it and become exit code 2 with a message naming the allowed values; and the whole output set is written by one function, so a path that returns early cannot emit four of six and leave a consumer reading a stale value for the other two. The entrypoint had no test of any kind: it has fourteen now, run against the real script with the CLI shimmed.
defects.not_shipped_because: the action is an integration definition in this tree, not a service running anywhere; nothing has ever executed it outside its own tests

defects.title: The encoding of what the tool prints came from the host's locale
defects.effect:
`sys.stdout`'s encoding is chosen from the locale, and nothing in this tool was deciding it. `actaira --lang es scan > report.txt` therefore wrote UTF-8 on a POSIX host with a UTF-8 locale and cp1252 on a default Windows install - the same command, over the same artifact, producing two different files, with the line endings differing too. A consumer reading the redirected output as UTF-8 got mojibake, and a character with no mapping in the host code page would have been a `UnicodeEncodeError` traceback out of a command that had already finished its work. Byte-level reproducibility is the property this repository spends a release gate defending everywhere else, and standard output was the one surface where nothing defended it. Redirected output is UTF-8 with `
` endings now, on every platform; a terminal keeps its own code page, because forcing UTF-8 into a console that is not expecting it renders mojibake, and gains `errors='replace'` so an undrawable character can never become a traceback.
defects.found_by: using the tool as a person would

defects.title: The localised screenshots were never localised: both READMEs showed the same image
defects.effect: `scripts/screenshots.py` selected the interface language only when it was not English, on the assumption that an unprimed page shows English. It does not: with no stored preference `app.js` follows `navigator.language`. So the language of every capture was whatever the browser running playwright happened to prefer, and the English and Spanish captures of a panel were byte-identical files - `04-governance.png` and `06-governance-es.png` the same image, `05-governance-dark.png` and `08-governance-dark-es.png` the same image, one of the two READMEs showing a screenshot in the other's language and neither saying so. `scripts/release_check.py` treats the two as one slot with a comment reading 'a localised README should show the localised screenshot', so the intent was written down in the gate while the generator never delivered it, and nothing compared the bytes. The language is selected in every case now, English included. Found by noticing that two files the pass had just written had identical sizes.
defects.not_shipped_because: a defect in the documentation the tool ships with rather than in the tool: the interface itself switches language correctly, which is what `tests/test_i18n.py` asserts

defects.title: The nightly's only check on the trojan's callable asserted the POSIX spelling of a platform-dependent name
defects.effect: `os.system` pickles under the name of the module `os` is implemented by on the machine that wrote the artifact: `posix.system` on Linux and macOS, `nt.system` on Windows. `test_the_real_trojan_names_posix_system_in_its_imports` asserted `posix.system` and nothing else, and its docstring said 'on this platform' about a property of the writing platform rather than of the format. Run with the real ML stack on Windows it failed against a report that was entirely correct - the worst kind of red, because a genuine regression in the one test that checks the trojan is named would have looked exactly the same. The expected name is derived from the interpreter now. The test also gained the assertion that was missing and matters more: that the DENYLIST flags it too. The allowlist fails closed and would refuse the name whichever way it was spelt; `--policy known-bad` only catches what it enumerates, so a denylist exercised only against `posix.system` is exactly where a Windows-authored gadget would have walked through. It does catch it - `nt` is in DENIED_MODULES beside `posix` - and that is now checked rather than assumed.
defects.not_shipped_because: the shipped tool is correct on both policies and on both spellings; this was a test that could only ever have been run on one kind of host, and an untested branch of the denylist

defects.title: The read bounded to protect memory allocated its whole ceiling for every file
defects.effect: `io_budget.read_at_most` called `handle.read(limit + 1)`. That is correct, and CPython allocates the requested size up front and then shrinks the object to what it actually read - so every pickle asked the allocator for 512 MiB before reading its bytes, a 16-byte one exactly as much as a real checkpoint, and every GGUF header asked for 64 MiB. On Linux the allocation is lazy and the pages are never touched, which is why this lived through five releases and a CI job that only ever ran on Linux. On a platform that commits what it allocates it costs about 78 ms per artifact and a real 512 MiB spike: `make benchmark` on Windows measured a median of 66 ms per file where the recorded Linux run of the same corpus measured 0.175 ms, and a scan of the 64-artifact corpus spent four and a half seconds in the allocator. The module's own docstring is what makes this more than a slow path - it exists so that 'a file that makes the auditor run out of memory is a file that does not get audited' cannot happen, and the bound it introduced was allocating the ceiling for every file regardless of size. The budget is a decision about the format; the allocation is now a fact about the file, from `os.fstat` on the already-open handle so there is no window in which the file could be replaced between the two. Median per artifact went from 70.0 ms to 0.568 ms on the machine that found it. Found by running `make benchmark` with the real rival tools on a platform the project had never measured on.

defects.title: Every data source in every graph drew as an unrecognised kind, silently
defects.effect: The graph renderer reads a node's kind from the prefix of its id and colours the box with it. The agent engine has emitted data sources as `data:<name>` since the declaration format was published; the renderer's vocabulary calls that kind `datasource`. So the prefix matched nothing, every data source fell to the `unknown` style, and the one node kind an attack-path reader most needs to pick out - the place untrusted content comes from - was drawn as the kind the renderer has no name for. Nothing failed: an unrecognised kind is still drawn, just neutrally, so there was no console error, no failed request and nothing for the screenshot gate to catch. The picture was simply wrong. Renaming either side would have meant changing a published node id or a stylesheet class to settle a spelling, so there is an explicit alias table instead, and the test is deliberately not about that one entry: it collects the prefixes the engine can actually emit and requires each to be classifiable, so the next id prefix somebody adds is caught the same way.
defects.found_by: writing a test for an adjacent feature

defects.title: `impact` answered that nothing depended on an agent's tools, because nothing joined them to it
defects.effect: `Agent.relations()` emits what the declaration says about its parts - the model, a tool's identity, a tool's inputs and outputs, an MCP server's exposed tools, a delegation - and it does not emit an edge from the agent to the tools and servers it declares. The shipped example has five tools, two MCP servers, one identity and two data sources, and contributed exactly one edge to the stored asset graph. So `actaira impact tool:fetch_url` reported nothing affected, and `actaira impact mcp:github` reported nothing affected, over a workspace whose manifest says a system uses an agent that declares both. A wrong answer, not a missing feature: the question was asked, the tool answered it, and the answer was the most reassuring one available. The fix is declaration-backed and lives at the graph-build layer: an agent declaration listing a tool is that declaration stating the agent has that tool, and the edge is read off the document rather than inferred from a name. Deliberately not added to `Agent.relations()`, because that feeds `to_bom()` and therefore `Agent.digest` - the number that answers 'is this the agent that was approved?' - which must not move because the graph wanted better connectivity.

defects.title: `watch` measured a local artifact's digest, compared against it, and then stored neither the digest nor any evidence about it
defects.effect: The filesystem connector publishes no `declared_sha256` by design (D-85b): a digest this tool computed and then compared against itself is not a check, so the field stays empty and `measured_sha256` carries what was actually read. `_write` and `_record_evidence` both consulted `declared_sha256` alone. The consequence on a local source, which is the commonest workspace there is, was that every artifact asset row was stored with an empty `digest` column and no per-artifact evidence record was written at all - while the same run used the measured digest to correctly report CONTENT_DRIFT. The measurement existed and was discarded one line before it was written down. Everything downstream reads that column: supersession is bound to a subject's digest (D-223), so there was nothing to supersede and a changed model invalidated nothing; `state.record.resolve` finds a scanned file by its digest, so no scan could ever be filed against a locally observed artifact; and the graph panel showed a digest-less node. The fix is one helper, `watch.artifact_digest`, that returns the strongest digest a snapshot holds - measured before declared - together with the basis it came from, so the two claims stay distinguishable in the asset attributes and in the evidence payload rather than being merged into one field that reads as identity.
defects.found_by: using the tool as a person would

defects.title: DEF-74's fix has never worked on Windows, because a URI was parsed with a string slice
defects.effect: `snapshot._measure` turned a `file:` URI into a path with `uri[len('file://'):]`. On POSIX that is right by coincidence. On Windows `file:///C:/models/w.bin` becomes `/C:/models/w.bin`, which is not a path that exists, so `is_file()` was false, `_measure` returned an empty string, and no local artifact was ever measured. Comparison then fell back to size - which is precisely the DEF-74 failure DEF-74 exists to prevent: a weight file replaced with different bytes of the same length comes back UNCHANGED, exit 0. It also mishandled percent-escapes on every platform, so a directory with a space in its name was never measured either. The regression test written for DEF-74 did not catch any of it, because its fixture assembled `file://` plus a native path by hand and that spelling is the one shape the old slice happened to survive; the connector emits `Path.as_uri()`, which it did not. The fix is `urllib.request.url2pathname`, which is per-platform by construction, with the hand-assembled spelling still accepted so that a URI written by a person does not silently fall back to a byte count. The fixture now uses the spelling the connector actually produces.
defects.found_by: using the tool as a person would
